content: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends screening donated blood for transfusion-transmissible infections to ensure safety. Chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection testing should focus on populations at higher risk, such as those with symptoms, clinical signs, or laboratory markers indicative of infection. Periodic re-testing using HCV nucleic acid testing (NAT) is advised for individuals with ongoing risk of acquisition or reinfection. In general populations with an HCV antibody seroprevalence of ≥2% or ≥5%, all adults should have access to HCV serological testing, with linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services. Testing strategies should leverage existing communityor facility-based programs, such as HIV or tuberculosis clinics, drug treatment services, and antenatal clinics. For specific birth cohorts of older individuals at higher risk of HCV infection and morbidity, targeted testing may be applied, even in populations with lower overall prevalence. Chronic HCV infection may be indicated by clinical evidence of liver disease, such as cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), or unexplained liver abnormalities, including abnormal liver function tests or imaging findings. Testing thresholds for HCV seroprevalence (≥2% or ≥5%) are based on published data and should be adapted to the country’s epidemiological context. Routine HCV testing of pregnant women is not currently recommended. Historical exposure to unscreened or inadequately screened blood products and unsafe injection practices are significant risk factors for infection. For infants, a complete hepatitis B vaccination schedule, including a birth dose, should be administered. Testing exposed infants for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) between 6 and 12 months of age is recommended to screen for infection. Acute hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection can be confirmed by detecting HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc, while chronic HBV infection is diagnosed by the persistence of HBsAg for six months or more. Laboratory-based immunoassays, such as enzyme immunoassay (EIA), chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA), and electrochemiluminescence assay (ECL), are recommended for diagnosing chronic HBV infection. These assays should meet WHO prequalification standards or stringent regulatory criteria and be used according to manufacturers’ instructions. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are recommended in settings with limited laboratory access to improve linkage to care and treatment. A single serological assay for HBsAg detection is recommended before further evaluation for HBV DNA and liver disease staging. Confirmation of HBsAg positivity may involve a neutralization step or a second different RDT assay. For HBV DNA detection, quantitative or qualitative NAT is recommended following a positive HBsAg test to guide treatment decisions. Monitoring for HBV treatment response and disease progression should include annual assessments of alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV DNA levels, as well as non-invasive tests like the aspartate-to-platelet ratio index (APRI) or transient elastography to evaluate for cirrhosis. Adherence to treatment should be regularly monitored, especially in individuals with advanced liver disease, HIV co-infection, or fluctuating ALT and HBV DNA levels. For HCV testing, serological assays (antibody or antibody/antigen) using RDTs or laboratory-based formats are recommended for detecting past or present infection in individuals older than 18 months. In children under 18 months, HCV infection can only be confirmed by virological assays detecting HCV RNA due to the presence of maternal antibodies. Following a reactive HCV antibody test, NAT for HCV RNA is the preferred strategy to diagnose viremia. Alternatively, assays detecting HCV core antigen with comparable sensitivity to NAT may be used. To improve testing uptake and linkage to care, facilityand community-based hepatitis testing services should implement evidence-based interventions, such as peer and lay health worker support in community settings and clinician reminders in facilities with electronic records. The global burden of hepatitis B and C remains disproportionately high in lowand middle-income countries, with most infected individuals unaware of their status. Enhanced testing strategies and access to effective treatments, such as direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) for HCV and long-term suppressive therapy for HBV, are critical to addressing this public health challenge.
